data.name: Cmd.ls.Summary
data.value: List the files and folders in a folder

data.name: Cmd.ls.Details
data.value:
Lists what is inside a folder. Without a path it lists the folder you are in.
-a also show hidden files (names starting with a dot) -l long format: permissions, owner, size and date
Flags can be combined: 'ls -la' shows everything in long format.

data.name: Cmd.cd.Summary
data.value: Change directory – move into another folder

data.name: Cmd.cd.Details
data.value:
Moves you into another folder.
cd <folder> move into a folder cd .. go up one level cd ~ go back to your home folder (so does plain 'cd') cd / go to the very top of the file system (the root)

data.name: Cmd.pwd.Summary
data.value: Print working directory – show where you are

data.name: Cmd.pwd.Details
data.value: Shows the full path of the folder you are in right now. Paths starting with / are absolute: they start at the very top of the file system.

data.name: Cmd.pwd.Example1
data.value: Show the current folder

data.name: Cmd.cat.Summary
data.value: Show what is inside a file

data.name: Cmd.cat.Details
data.value:
Prints the contents of one or more files. The name is short for 'concatenate' – it can glue several files together.
-n number every line

data.name: Cmd.cat.Example1

data.name: Cmd.cat.Example2

data.name: Cmd.grep.Summary
data.value: Search for text inside files

data.name: Cmd.grep.Details
data.value:
Prints every line that contains the text you are looking for. Perfect for digging through big log files.
-i ignore upper and lower case -n show line numbers -v invert: show the lines that do NOT match -r search every file in a folder and its subfolders
You can also send the output of another command into grep with a pipe (|).

data.name: Cmd.head.Summary
data.value: Show the first lines of a file

data.name: Cmd.head.Details
data.value:
Prints the first 10 lines of a file or of piped input – a quick peek without scrolling through everything.
-n <lines> how many lines to show ('head -5' works too)

data.name: Cmd.head.Example1

data.name: Cmd.head.Example2

data.name: Cmd.tail.Summary
data.value: Show the last lines of a file

data.name: Cmd.tail.Details
data.value:
Prints the last 10 lines of a file or of piped input. Logs grow at the bottom, so tail shows the newest events.
-n <lines> how many lines to show ('tail -1' works too)

data.name: Cmd.tail.Example1
data.value: The newest 10 lines of the system log

data.name: Cmd.tail.Example2
data.value: Only the very last line

data.name: Cmd.wc.Summary
data.value: Count lines, words and characters

data.name: Cmd.wc.Details
data.value:
Word count: counts the lines, words and bytes (characters) in a file or in piped input.
-l only count lines -w only count words -c only count bytes
'wc -l' at the end of a pipe answers "how many?" – how many failed logins, how many files, how many users.

data.name: Cmd.wc.Example3
data.value: How many files are in /etc?

data.name: Cmd.sort.Summary
data.value: Sort lines alphabetically or by number

data.name: Cmd.sort.Details
data.value:
Sorts the lines of a file or of piped input.
-r reverse: largest or last first -n sort by the number at the start of each line (so 10 comes after 9) -u remove duplicate lines
Without -n, sorting is letter by letter: '10' comes before '9', and capital letters before small ones.

data.name: Cmd.sort.Example1
data.value: The users in alphabetical order

data.name: Cmd.sort.Example2
data.value: The same, in reverse order

data.name: Cmd.sort.Example3
data.value: Which login shells the users have, the most common first

data.name: Cmd.uniq.Summary
data.value: Remove or count repeated lines

data.name: Cmd.uniq.Details
data.value:
Collapses repeated lines that come right after each other into one. That is why it is almost always used after sort: sorting puts identical lines next to each other.
-c put the number of repeats in front of each line
The classic way to find what occurs most often: sort | uniq -c | sort -n

data.name: Cmd.uniq.Example1
data.value: Every login shell, each listed once

data.name: Cmd.uniq.Example2
data.value: How many users have each login shell

data.name: Cmd.cut.Summary
data.value: Pick out columns (fields) from each line

data.name: Cmd.cut.Details
data.value:
Splits every line at a delimiter character and keeps only the fields (columns) you ask for. Fields are numbered from 1.
-d <char> the delimiter, e.g. -d: or -d' ' for a space (default: tab) -f <fields> which fields: -f1, -f1,3 (field 1 and 3) or -f2-4 (field 2 to 4)
Lines without the delimiter are printed unchanged.

data.value: Only the user names from /etc/passwd

data.name: Cmd.cut.Example2
data.value: User names and their home folders

data.name: Cmd.cut.Example3
data.value: Field 5 of each log line: the program that wrote it

data.name: Cmd.echo.Summary
data.value: Print text

data.name: Cmd.echo.Details
data.value:
Prints the text you give it. Mostly useful to send a piece of text into another command with a pipe.
-n no line break at the end
Put text with spaces or special characters in quotes: echo 'a | b'

data.name: Cmd.echo.Example1

data.name: Cmd.echo.Example2
data.value: Send text into another command

data.name: Cmd.base64.Summary
data.value: Encode or decode base64 text

data.name: Cmd.base64.Details
data.value:
Base64 writes any data using only letters, digits, + and / (often with = at the end). It is used to send data through systems that only handle plain text.
-d decode: turn base64 back into the original
Base64 is an encoding, NOT encryption: there is no key or password, so anyone can decode it.

data.name: Cmd.history.Summary
data.value: Show the commands you have typed

data.name: Cmd.history.Details
data.value:
Lists the commands you have run, oldest first, with a number in front. Add a number to only see the latest ones.
-c clear the history
On a real computer the history is saved in ~/.bash_history – a file investigators (and attackers) love to read.

data.name: Cmd.find.Summary
data.value: Search for files and folders by name

data.name: Cmd.find.Details
data.value:
Searches through folders for files and folders.
find <name> quick search everywhere for names containing <name> find <path> -name <pat> search below <path>; * matches anything, ? one character -iname <pat> like -name, but ignores upper and lower case -type f / -type d only files / only folders
Folders you are not allowed to open are reported as 'Permission denied'.

data.name: Cmd.su.Summary
data.value: Switch user – become someone else (if you know the password)

data.name: Cmd.su.Details
data.value:
Lets you act as another user. You have to type that user's password; the letters are not shown while you type. Without a name, su tries to become root.
su <user> become <user> and stay in the same folder su - <user> become <user> and go to their home folder exit go back to the user you were before
On a real computer you may only do this with permission – just like everything else in Hackdot.

data.name: Cmd.sudo.Summary
data.value: Run one command as root – if the sudo rules allow it

data.name: Cmd.sudo.Details
data.value:
"Superuser do": runs a single command as root. Unlike su, you don't need root's password – the file /etc/sudoers decides which users may run which commands.
sudo -l list the commands you may run as root sudo <command> ... run the command as root
A rule like '/usr/bin/cat /var/log/*' looks harmless, but * matches any text – even '..' – so it can open far more than intended.
